title: Ed Davey rejects claims party is ‘sleepwalking into irrelevance’ under his leadership – UK politics live
summary:
Lib Dem leader says he is proud of party’s record at Brighton conference

Ed Davey has urged Andy Burnham to deliver some “home truths” to Donald Trump when they meet at the…

blocks.text: Ed Davey rejects claims party is 'sleepwalking into irrelevance' under his leadership

Good morning. Ed Davey became Lib Dem leader in 2020, which means he is technically the longest-serving leader of a national party in the UK. (“Technically” because, while Nigel Farage only became leader of Reform UK in his current incumbency in 2024, he had led it before when it was called the Brexit party and, if you include Ukip, he has been leader of the anti-migrant, anti-EU right in British politics for more than 20 years.) After six years in charge, it is inevitable that some Lib Dems are starting to complain and, with the Lib Dem conference taking place in Brighton, Davey has been giving interviews this morning where he has had to respond to complaints from his critics.
The most vocal has been Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon county council, who told the BBC yesterday that the Lib Dems were “sleepwalking into irrelevance” with Davey at the helm.
Not surprisingly, Davey does not agree.
Asked about Brazil’s comments, the Lib Dem leader told BBC Breakfast:

double quotation markWe’ve grown really fast in recent years under my leadership. Record number of MPs. We’re running more councils than the Conservatives – councils up and down the country. [I’m] really proud of that record and it means when you have a bigger party, you can’t please everyone all the time.
And Davey was a bit more blunt when asked the same question on Sky News.

double quotation markI would say to the Devon councillor, we’ve now got six Liberal Democrat MPs in Devon. That’s not happened since the 1920s. We have a huge number of councillors across Devon and are leading the way in Devon, and I could go around the rest of the country. I happen to know Brazil. We’ve rarely seen eye to eye. So, all I would say is, we’re going to build on the success we’ve had.
I will post more from Davey’s interviews shortly.
There is more coverage here of what was happening at the Lib Dem conference at the weekend.
Here is the agenda for the day.

blocks.text: Davey urges Burnham to 'take a stand' when PM meets Trump in New York tomorrow
Ed Davey has urged Andy Burnham to deliver some “home truths” to Donald Trump when they meet at the UN tomorrow.
Asked how Burnham should treat the US president, Davey told Sky News:
double quotation markTake a stand, please. And the cosying up to him that was done by Keir Starmer absolutely failed miserably.
Davey praised Mark Carney, the Liberal Canadian PM for “standing up to Trump with success” and, referring to what he wanted to see from Burnham, he said:

double quotation markYou have to stand up to them. And this is a man who’s ruining our world. He’s ruining his own country, but he’s hitting people in our country. His disastrous war in Iran is leading to the hike in oil and gas prices, which means people are paying more for petrol and diesel. So if Andy Burnham is going to represent Britain’s interests and the interests of British people, he needs to tell Donald Trump some home truths, whether it’s on the economy and defence, whether it’s on Iran, whether it’s on NATO. I’m afraid, under President Trump, we no longer have a reliable ally in the White House ... You can’t trust this man. And I think, while he may want to choose his words slightly more diplomatically than I’m giving to you, he needs to stand up for Britain and British interests.

With Trump deeply unpopular in the UK, it is easy to see why Davey criticises him harshly. But prime ministers who have had to negotiate with Trump have tended to be more tactful and, in her preview of what is likely to happen when Burnham meets Trump tomorrow, Pippa Crerar, the Guardian’s political editor, says Burnham is not angling for a fight. She says:

double quotation markDowning Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful [than Keir Starmer was] when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister. Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.
